Patient demographics:
  age: 50
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing

Vignette:
Terrell had been working a routine emergency call in a rowhouse on the South Side when the homeowner, agitated and armed, turned on him. The assault happened in a narrow utility closet: a sudden swing, a heavy impact against his ribs, the sharp crack of a wrench slipping from his grip. What frightened him most was not the pain, but the silence that followed, the way the attacker vanished into the alley, leaving him pressed against damp drywall. He tried to explain the night to his wife, Elena, but the words caught in his throat. Every time he opened his mouth, only a sequence of still, sharp images surfaced—the glint of metal in a sliver of hallway light, the heavy shadow falling across his boots, the crumpled position of his own body against the pipe rack. Whenever those pictures returned, a heavy shame settled in his chest, as if he had failed to protect himself when he should have. He was certain that speaking it out loud would only fracture him further, so he stopped trying. In the weeks that followed, the house grew smaller. He stopped using the guest bathroom because the mirror made him watch his own reflection too closely. The only rooms where his chest stopped tight were the master bedroom with the deadbolt thrown and his own tool shed, where the door clicked shut and the air smelled of oil and copper. At the job site, a sudden shift of weight by a coworker reaching over a sink or a dropped wrench clattering against concrete sent his shoulders into a rigid brace, his hands flying up as if warding off a blow that wasn’t there. Nights brought no relief. He would lie in bed, staring at the ceiling, waiting for his breathing to slow, but his mind kept replaying the closet—the way the floor tilted, the sudden impact, the lingering pressure on his ribs. When he finally drifted off, a floorboard settling upstairs or the neighbor’s dog barking would snap him awake, his heart hammering against his sternum. He told himself he was just getting older, but Elena noticed how he flinched when she moved too quickly across the kitchen. Plumbing had been his trade for twenty-two years, the work that gave him pride and steady checks. Now, stepping into a crawlspace felt like walking onto a stage where he might trip again. He had come to believe he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him, that his hands had forgotten how to trust their own judgment. When he did take a job, he found himself pausing over every joint, questioning whether he had tightened the fitting enough, whether he had missed a warning sign. He couldn’t trust that he would do the right thing when something went sideways. He kept returning the case to the dispatcher, citing equipment issues, though the truth sat heavy in his gut. He kept returning to that same thought: what happened to him was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. The man who did it was gone, the report filed, and Terrell was left to carry the weight of a broken system alone. The turning point came three months ago when he missed a critical shut-off valve during a routine call, leaving a family without water for two days. Elena had found him sitting in his truck in the parking lot of a hardware store, knuckles white on the steering wheel, unable to step out. That night, he sat at the kitchen table and laid out the intake paperwork the clinic had sent. He was tired of the locked doors, the startled gasps that followed him down streets, the sleepless hours that turned his mornings gray. He had come to believe that if he never spoke of it, he could keep it contained, but the containment was fraying. He went to the intake clinic hoping someone might finally see the unfairness of what was left undone, and maybe, just maybe, help him find a way to walk through a room without bracing for a blow that was no longer there.
